definition: Precursor means something that came before and led to the development of another thing.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word precursor. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know precursor should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The abacus was a precursor to the modern calculator, working out sums centuries before electronics existed.
Predecessor is weaker — it only says something held the spot earlier, with no claim that it shaped what came next; a precursor actively led to the later development.
Progenitor is stronger — it names the direct source or originator from which something descends, while a precursor merely ran ahead and paved the way.

A forerunner ran ahead and signaled what was coming — the word pictures a runner out in front. It stresses the announcing. A precursor stresses the leading-to: it came before and actually fed the later development. The words overlap heavily, but forerunner points at the signal, while a precursor helped bring about what followed.

An antecedent is simply the earlier item in a sequence — in grammar, the noun a pronoun refers back to; in history, whatever came before. It is neutral about influence. A precursor is an antecedent with a causal claim attached: it came earlier and led toward the later thing, paving its way.

A prototype is a working trial model of the very thing being developed — an unfinished early version of the same product. A precursor is a separate, complete thing from an earlier era that paved the way for a later one. The first test iPhone was a prototype; the telegraph was a precursor of instant messaging.

Precursor means something that came before and led to the development of another thing.
Film historians treat the silent newsreel as a precursor to today's televised evening news.
The silent newsreel came first and directly shaped what followed — that two-part relationship (earlier + led to the later thing) is exactly what makes something a precursor, not merely something old.
Precursor usually appears in writing about the history of science, technology, music, or ideas, and is typically followed by 'to' or 'of' ('a precursor to the internet').
It always points forward from the earlier thing — never call the later invention a precursor of the earlier one.

Before the refrigerator hummed in every kitchen, there was the icebox: an insulated oak cabinet cooled by a block of ice delivered to the door each week.
Historians of technology describe the icebox as a precursor of the modern refrigerator, and the debt runs deeper than the name.
The icebox trained households to expect fresh milk and meat at home, created the cold-storage habit, and built the delivery networks that early refrigerator companies later used.
When electric models arrived in the 1920s, they slid into a space — in the kitchen and in daily routine — that the icebox had already carved out.
The machines shared no parts; what passed between them was a path.
